newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia says Russian peacekeepers must do more.
newsitem.headline: Georgia says Russian peacekeepers must do more.

text.p: President Eduard Shevardnadze on Monday warned that Russia's peacekeeping forces in the breakaway Georgian region of Abkhazia must do more or leave.
Shevardnadze said he will insist on significant changes to the 2,500-strong force's mandate when he meets other leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) on March 28 in Moscow.

"The summit must take up a new mandate for the peacekeepers. If this doesn't happen, then the parliament's decision will be put on the table," the former Soviet foreign minister said in his weekly radio address.

Shevardnadze was referring to a resolution by parliament earlier this month calling the three-year old Russian mission "a complete failure" and demanding the troops be pulled out by June if the scope of their activities was not widened.

It demands the zone the peacekeepers patrol be expanded by several kilometers (miles) deeper into Abkhazia, and for them to help with the return of more than 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees who fled in 1993 after separatists took over.

A war between disorganised Georgian troops and Abkhaz irregulars, backed by military help from Russia, killed more than 10,000 soldiers and civilians from 1992-93. Georgia sent in forces in August 1992 to quell local demands for more autonomy.
Russian support for the Abkhaz came at a time of poor relations between Moscow and Tbilisi.
Foreign Minister Irakly Menagarishvili told Reuters that Georgia also wanted better implementation of CIS sanctions imposed against Abkhazia in 1996.

Russia's warships patrol the Abkhaz Black Sea coast and its border guards control its only land access to the outside world, but Georgia says enforcement of sanctions limiting movement of goods and people to and from Abkhazia is spotty.
It also wants telephone and postal links from Russia to the region cut.
The Abkhaz say the measures are aimed at "psychological torture" of its people.
Russia faces a dilemma in Abkhazia as Georgia's discontent with their peacekeeping is matched by Abkhaz outrage over what it calls Moscow's military and financial support for Georgia.
The parliament of the self-styled republic on Friday called for negotiations with Tbilisi to be suspended until sanctions are lifted, and said further Russian mediation was pointless.
It said the return of Georgian refugees, who once accounted for 45 percent of Abkhazia's population, should be suspended.
But Vladislav Ardzinba, the Abkhaz leader who enjoys wide powers, said he did not favour a break in talks.
Relations between Georgia and Russia have taken a new turn for the worse in recent months.
Shevardnadze recently said that Moscow would had to give up three military bases it holds in the republic unless it can help reassert Tbilisi's control over Abkhazia.

Several thousand people, many refugees from Abkhazia, held a noisy rally in the center of Tbilisi on Friday demanding a Russian withdrawal. Ten lawmakers have been on hunger strike for more than two weeks demanding the troops leave.
